**Gauss's law** does not care how many kinds of charge exist - it depends only on the
charge **enclosed**.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
∮Ē·d̄s̄ = **q_enclosed/ε₀** ✓
**Step 2 — see what it requires.** Only that charge be a conserved scalar producing an
inverse-square field ✓ Nothing in the derivation assumes two signs.
**Step 3 — apply it to a one-sign universe.** The law holds exactly as before:
**zero** flux if no charge is inside ✓
**q/ε₀** if charge is inside ✓
**Why the flux is zero for an external charge.** Every field line entering the closed
surface must also **leave** it ✓ The inward and outward contributions cancel exactly,
whatever the charge outside - and that argument makes no reference to sign.
**Why the first option is wrong.** It claims the flux is non-zero on **any** surface ✓
But a surface enclosing no charge has zero flux, one-sign universe or not.
**Why the second option is wrong.** The integral is perfectly well **defined** ✓ Flux
is a mathematical construction from the field and the surface; it exists wherever a
field does.
**Why the third option is wrong.** The flux is q/ε₀ - **finite** ✓ It would be infinite
only for an infinite enclosed charge.
**What would really change in such a universe.** Everything would **repel** everything
else ✓ No atoms, no molecules, no neutral matter - the universe would fly apart. But
Gauss's law, as a statement about fields and charges, would remain exactly true.
**Why the law is so general.** It follows from the **inverse-square** nature of the
field and nothing else ✓ Gravity obeys an identical law, with mass in place of charge -
and mass comes in only **one** sign, which is itself a demonstration that one-sign
Gauss's law is perfectly consistent.
**Why Gauss's law is so useful.** With enough **symmetry** it yields E at once, with no
integration ✓ the field of a sphere, a line, a plane, a cylinder - each in two lines.
**The magnetic counterpart.** ∮B̄·d̄s̄ = **0** always ✓ because no magnetic monopole
exists. That is the one case where a Gauss-type law really is changed by the absence of
a kind of "charge".
∴ ∮E·ds = 0 if charge is outside, = q/ε₀ if charge is inside.

Uniform acceleration **eE/m** over a distance h, so **h = ½at²**.
**Step 1 — find the acceleration.**
a = **eE/m** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the distance formula.** The electron starts from rest:
h = ½at²
= ½(eE/m)t² ✓
**Step 3 — solve for t.**
t² = 2hm/(eE)
**t = √(2hm/eE)** ✓
**The dimensional check.**
[hm/eE] = (m)(kg)/[(C)(N C⁻¹)] = (m kg)/(N) = (m kg)/(kg m s⁻²) = **s²** ✓ so the
square root is a time, and the options without the root fail at once.
**Why the second and fourth options are impossible.** They have **no square root** ✓
2hm/eE has units of s², not s - a dimensional check disposes of both in a moment.
**Why the third option is upside down.** √(2eE/hm) has units of 1/s ✓ a frequency, not
a time.
**The analogy with free fall.** Replace eE/m by g and the formula becomes
t = **√(2h/g)** ✓ the familiar result. The electric case is identical in structure,
with eE/m playing the part of g.
**How much larger the electric acceleration is.** For E = 1000 V m⁻¹:
a = (1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)(1000)/(9·1 x 10⁻³¹) = **1·76 x 10¹⁴ m s⁻²** ✓
some **10¹³ times** g - which is why gravity is always neglected for charged particles
in laboratory fields.
**A worked time.** Over h = 1 cm in that field:
t = √(2 x 0·01/1·76 x 10¹⁴) = **3·4 x 10⁻⁹ s** ✓ a few nanoseconds, and the electron
arrives at 6 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
**The final speed, for completeness.**
v = √(2eEh/m) ✓ and v = at, consistent with the time found.
**Why the field must be uniform.** Only then is the acceleration **constant** and the
simple kinematic formula valid ✓ A non-uniform field would require integration.
**Where this calculation is used.** In the **deflecting plates** of a cathode-ray tube
and in every electron gun ✓ The transit time sets the highest frequency such a device
can follow.
∴ t = √(2hm/eE).

On the axis the dipole field is **twice** as strong as on the equator and points the
**opposite** way.
**Step 1 — write the two fields.** For r ≫ a,
**axial**: E_ax = 2kp/r³, directed **along** p̄ ✓
**equatorial**: E_eq = kp/r³, directed **opposite** to p̄ ✓
**Step 2 — compare magnitudes.**
|E_ax| = **2|E_eq|** ✓
**Step 3 — compare directions.** They are **antiparallel** ✓
**Step 4 — combine into one statement.**
**Ē_ax = −2Ē_eq** ✓
**Why the axial field is the stronger.** On the axis the near charge is closer and the
far one further, and their contributions **partly reinforce** after the subtraction ✓
On the equator both charges are equidistant and their vertical components **cancel**,
leaving only the horizontal components - half as much.
**Why the equatorial field opposes p̄.** At an equatorial point the horizontal
components both point from the **positive** charge towards the **negative** one ✓ that
is, **against** the dipole moment, which by convention runs from −q to +q.
**The derivation, briefly.**
axial: kq/(r − a)² − kq/(r + a)² ≈ **4kqa/r³ = 2kp/r³** ✓
equatorial: 2 x [kq/(r² + a²)] x [a/√(r² + a²)] ≈ **kqa/r³ = kp/r³** ✓
**Why both fall as 1/r³.** The two charges nearly cancel at large distance ✓ leaving
only the **difference** of two inverse squares, which goes as the inverse cube. A
dipole's influence dies away much faster than a single charge's.
**A worked instance.** A dipole of p = 10⁻²⁹ C m at r = 1 nm:
E_ax = 2(9 x 10⁹)(10⁻²⁹)/10⁻²⁷ = **1·8 x 10⁸ V m⁻¹** ✓
E_eq = **9 x 10⁷ V m⁻¹** ✓ exactly half, and oppositely directed.
**At a general angle.** E = (kp/r³)√(1 + 3cos²θ) ✓ which gives 2kp/r³ at θ = 0 and
kp/r³ at θ = 90° - the two special cases above.
**Why this matters.** Water molecules are dipoles, and the 1/r³ falloff with its
angular dependence governs **hydrogen bonding**, solvation and the structure of
liquids ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **E_ax = E_eq** ✗ ignores both the factor of 2 and the
sign. **E_ax = −E_eq** ✗ has the direction right but not the magnitude.
**E_eq = 2E_ax** ✗ inverts the factor ✓
∴ Ē_ax = − 2 Ē_eq.

The potential of a point charge depends only on **r**, so the equipotentials are
**concentric spheres**.
**Step 1 — write the potential.**
V = **kq/r** ✓
**Step 2 — find the surfaces of constant V.** V is the same wherever **r** is the
same ✓ and the locus of points at a fixed distance from a point is a **sphere**
centred on that point.
**Step 3 — conclude.** A **sphere with the charge at its centre** ✓
**Why the charge must be at the centre.** Only then is every point of the surface
equidistant ✓ A sphere with the charge on its **surface** - the third option - has
points at distances from 0 to 2R, and so is not an equipotential at all.
**The essential property of an equipotential.** The field is everywhere
**perpendicular** to it ✓ Were there a tangential component, charge would flow along
the surface and the potential would not be constant.
**Why no work is done along one.**
W = qΔV = **0** ✓ Moving a charge anywhere on an equipotential costs nothing - which is
why a satellite in a **circular** orbit needs no fuel.
**The spacing of the surfaces.** For equal steps in V, the spheres crowd together near
the charge and spread out far away ✓ because V = kq/r changes rapidly at small r. Close
spacing means a **strong** field.
**Equipotentials in other geometries.**
a **uniform** field: parallel **planes** ✓
a long charged **wire**: coaxial **cylinders** ✓
a charged **conductor** of any shape: its own **surface**, and surfaces hugging it ✓
**Why a conductor's surface is always an equipotential.** Any potential difference
would drive a current along it ✓ In electrostatic equilibrium nothing flows, so the
whole conductor - surface and interior - sits at one potential.
**The field lines.** Always **perpendicular** to the equipotentials ✓ For a point
charge they are radial lines, meeting the concentric spheres at right angles
everywhere.
**Why two equipotentials can never cross.** The point of crossing would have two
different potentials ✓ an impossibility, exactly as two field lines cannot cross.
**Reading the distractors.** **Ellipsoid with charge at the foci** ✗ would be the
shape for a different field. **Sphere with charge on the surface** ✗ and **plane with
charge on the surface** ✗ both place the charge where r varies across the surface ✓
∴ Sphere with charge at the centre of the sphere.

The loss of **electrostatic potential energy** becomes kinetic energy.
**Step 1 — write the energy balance.**
kQq(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) = **½mv²** ✓
**Step 2 — evaluate kQq.**
kQq = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻³)(1 x 10⁻⁶)
= (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)
= **18 J m** ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate the bracket.**
1/1 − 1/10 = **0·9 m⁻¹** ✓
**Step 4 — find the kinetic energy.**
½mv² = 18 x 0·9
= **16·2 J** ✓
**Step 5 — solve for v.** With m = 1 g = **10⁻³ kg**:
v² = 2(16·2)/10⁻³
= **32400**
**v = 180 m s⁻¹** ✓
**Why the energy method is the only practical one.** The force **varies** as 1/r² along
the path ✓ so the acceleration is not constant and the kinematic formulas cannot be
used. Energy conservation sidesteps the whole difficulty.
**How much energy remains available.** At infinity the particle would reach
v = √(2 x 18/10⁻³) = **190 m s⁻¹** ✓ so 90% of the available energy is gained in the
first ten metres - the force falls off so fast that the rest contributes little.
**Why the mass must be in kilograms.** 1 g = **10⁻³ kg** ✓ Leaving it as 1 would give
v = 5·7 m s⁻¹, a factor of √1000 astray.
**A check on the potential energies.**
at 1 m: U = 18/1 = **18 J** ✓
at 10 m: U = 18/10 = **1·8 J** ✓
difference **16·2 J** ✓ exactly the kinetic energy gained.
**Why "frictionless" matters.** All the lost potential energy becomes kinetic ✓ With
friction, part would be dissipated and the speed would be less.
**How large these charges are.** 2 mC is an enormous charge ✓ Two such charges a metre
apart would repel with F = kQ²/r² = 36000 N. In practice such charges leak away
rapidly through the air.
**The sign of the work.** Both charges are **positive**, so they repel and the
potential energy **falls** as they separate ✓ The particle accelerates away - as the
question says.
**Reading the distractors.** **60**, **90** and **100 m s⁻¹** ✗ correspond to kinetic
energies of 1·8, 4·05 and 5 J ✓ Only 16·2 J, from the full 0·9 factor, gives 180 m s⁻¹.
∴ 180 ms⁻¹.

In the **steady state** no current flows in the capacitor branch, so there is no drop
across the 20 Ω.
**Step 1 — delete the capacitor branch for the current calculation.** A fully charged
capacitor passes **no** steady current ✓ so the 20 Ω in series with it carries nothing.
**Step 2 — find the current in the rest of the circuit.** The 5 V cell drives current
through its 1 Ω and the 4 Ω:
I = 5/(1 + 4)
= **1 A** ✓
**Step 3 — find the voltage across the 4 Ω.**
V = IR = 1 x 4 = **4 V** ✓
**Step 4 — find the capacitor's voltage.** The capacitor branch bridges the same two
nodes as the 4 Ω, and with no current there is **no drop** across the 20 Ω ✓ so the
whole 4 V appears across the capacitor.
**Step 5 — find the charge.**
Q = CV
= 8 x 4
= **32 C** ✓
**Why the 20 Ω is irrelevant.** It carries no current, so **V = IR = 0** across it ✓
Its only role is to limit the **charging** current when the circuit is first switched
on - once the steady state is reached, it might as well be a plain wire.
**Why the 1 Ω does matter.** It carries the main current and drops **1 V** ✓ leaving
only 4 V for the 4 Ω - which is what the capacitor sees.
**The transient, for completeness.** On switch-on the capacitor charges with time
constant
τ = RC, with R the Thevenin resistance seen by the capacitor ✓ Here that is
20 + (4 ∥ 1) = 20·8 Ω, so τ = **166 s** - a very slow charge, since 8 F is an enormous
capacitance.
**How large 8 F really is.** Colossal ✓ Ordinary capacitors are microfarads;
supercapacitors reach tens of farads. The question's value is chosen for arithmetic
convenience, and 32 C is correspondingly huge.
**The energy stored.**
U = ½CV² = ½(8)(16) = **64 J** ✓
**Why the capacitor's voltage is not the full 5 V.** The cell's internal resistance
drops 1 V ✓ Only the terminal voltage, 4 V, is available to the external network.
**Reading the distractors.** **40 C** ✗ uses the full 5 V, forgetting the internal
resistance. **80 C** ✗ doubles it, and **0 C** ✗ would need no voltage across the
capacitor at all ✓
∴ 32 C.

Mobility is **µ = eτ/m**, so it is **directly proportional to the relaxation time**.
**Step 1 — recall the definition.** Mobility is the drift velocity per unit field:
µ = **v_d/E** ✓
**Step 2 — write the drift velocity.**
v_d = **eEτ/m** ✓
with τ the mean time between collisions.
**Step 3 — combine.**
µ = (eEτ/m)/E
= **eτ/m** ✓ directly proportional to **τ**.
**Why the electron density does not appear.** µ describes how freely **one** electron
moves ✓ The number of electrons affects the **conductivity**,
σ = **neµ** ✓
but not the mobility of each.
**What τ depends on.** The frequency of collisions with lattice ions and impurities ✓
**Hotter** material: more vigorous vibrations, **smaller** τ, **lower** mobility ✓
**Purer** material: fewer impurity collisions, **larger** τ ✓
**Why metals conduct worse when hot.** τ falls, so µ falls, and with n fixed the
conductivity σ = neµ falls ✓ That is the whole explanation of a metal's positive
temperature coefficient.
**Typical values.**
copper: µ ≈ **4·4 x 10⁻³ m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹** ✓
silicon electrons: **0·135 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹** ✓ far higher per carrier, though silicon has
vastly fewer carriers.
**Why semiconductors have higher mobility but lower conductivity.** σ = neµ ✓ Their µ
is large but their n is smaller by many orders of magnitude, so σ is much less.
**The relaxation time's size.** About **10⁻¹⁴ s** in a metal ✓ so an electron suffers
some 10¹⁴ collisions a second - which is why the drift velocity is only millimetres
per second despite enormous thermal speeds.
**Why electrons and holes differ.** In silicon, electron mobility is about **three
times** hole mobility ✓ which is why n-channel transistors are faster than p-channel
ones, and why CMOS designs size the two differently.
**The units.** m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ ✓ from (m s⁻¹)/(V m⁻¹).
**Reading the distractors.** **Inversely proportional to relaxation time** ✗ reverses
the relation. The two options involving **electron density** ✗ confuse mobility with
conductivity ✓
∴ directly proportional to relaxation time.
